inputs.description: Computes due dates for a fictional lending service. Each clock is defined by a rule: an anchor event, a direction (before or after), an amount and unit (business days, days, hours, months), a boundary phrasing, a counting rule and a versioned holiday calendar. Examples: a reminder at least 3 business days before an item is due; an escalation within 10 business days of a missed return. The calculator computes and reminds; it never takes an act. Every computed date must carry the rule and calendar version that produced it. Seven acceptance cases are hand-worked (month-end, leap day, daylight saving, retroactive holiday designation). The forbidden states F1 to F7 must never occur.
inputs.decision_question_answers:
M1 Source of truth. Which artifact should win when artifacts disagree, what form can it take (prose, structured data, executable tests, a formal contract or model, or running code), and who or what changes it?
  Answer: split: clock records for what each deadline is; acceptance cases for how counting works (assumed)
M2 Knowability. Can correct behaviour be stated before building, or only discovered by building?
  Answer: knowable from the rules; exceptions flagged undetermined (tested)
M3 Requirements stability. How often will intent change, and is the change driven by learning or by outside rules?
  Answer: stable rules; change comes from outside (new holiday calendars, new locations) (assumed)
M4 Cost of being wrong and reversibility. What happens if it is built wrong, and how hard is it to undo?
  Answer: high; a wrong date can trigger a wrongful penalty; reversible in the record, not in the world (tested)
M5 Verifiability. How will we know it is correct: test, proof, inspection, measurement, use?
  Answer: high; every date can be hand-worked and compared (tested)
M6 Accountability. Must intent be provable later to a regulator, auditor, client or public?
  Answer: high; a reviewer must see the rule and calendar version behind any date (tested)
M7 Builder. Who or what does the building, and what inputs can that builder reliably use?
  Answer: AI agents, gated by tests (assumed)
M8 Lifespan. How long will this system live and be maintained?
  Answer: long; core of the service (assumed)
M9 Neighbours. What does it meet, which methodologies do those neighbours use, and what boundary contract is needed?
  Answer: rules, calendar and notification subsystems; boundary contract is the calculator's output record (tested)
M10 Switch conditions. What would make us change methodology?
  Answer: a clock that cannot be expressed as data drops to spec-anchored prose plus a flagged human decision (assumed)
M11 Evidence. Have we used this methodology on a similar system, and what happened?
  Answer: one case: hand-worked checks against real data caught a wrong rule (tested)

fits_met.c: High-stakes systems where failure is costly or unsafe (high cost of being wrong, strong accountability to a regulator or auditor)
Requirements are stable enough to write a test specification for each level before building (unit, integration, system, acceptance)
A verification phase can be planned in parallel with each design stage, so every specification has a test that checks it
Behaviour must stay coherent across many sessions and readers
Core invariants that must never break
Locking a handful of primary use cases with a stakeholder
High reliability is needed and behaviour can be stated as automated tests (high verifiability)
Any boundary between two systems or two agents
Requirements are fixed and well understood before building starts (high knowability, low expected change)
Frequent, small, reversible releases are wanted and supported by automated build, test and deploy (CI/CD)
Production behaviour can be monitored so that failures and slowdowns show up quickly
Several internal consumers whose needs diverge
Work can be cut into fixed-length sprints that each produce something a user can see or use
The team can fill the roles: a product owner who decides priority, a Scrum Master who guards the process, and developers who build
Large, complex or high-risk systems where the main uncertainties (technical, cost, schedule) can be named and reduced step by step
Each cycle can end with a review that decides whether to continue, change course or stop (high cost of being wrong, spending staged)
Prototypes or experiments can retire a risk before the next commitment is made
Killing bad ideas cheaply
Experience documents exist (users, jobs, journeys, objects, states) to design against

unfit_met.c: No human uses the system directly (a library, a protocol, a batch job)
A fixed, well-understood specification must be delivered exactly, so there is little waste to remove

fits_met.c: A slice with known acceptance criteria, done in one agent session

unfit_met.c: Intent that must stay true for months
The system is large, safety-critical or needs heavy documentation and formal verification (high cost of being wrong)
A prototype could be mistaken for the finished system and carry weak structure into a long-lived product (long lifespan)
